query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a modest amount of molybdenum (Mo) into the high-entropy alloy will enable the in situ formation of a lubricious MoO2 layer during sliding, thereby reducing both the friction coefficient and wear rate over a broad temperature range compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy used for self-lubricating moving components without Mo addition.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding a controlled fraction of Mo (by weight or atomic percent) during alloy synthesis to promote MoO2 formation at the friction interface.
generation.conditions: The modified and control samples are subjected to identical dry sliding wear tests under a range of service temperatures (from room temperature up to the high operational temperatures) and under matching load and speed conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The generation of a thin, self-adaptive, layered MoO2 oxide film at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: Under frictional heating, the Mo present in the alloy preferentially oxidizes to form a lubricious MoO2 layer. This film reduces interfacial shear stress by providing an easy-shear plane, while the overall improved hardness-toughness balance of the alloy mitigates material removal, both contributing to lower friction and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the primary measured properties: the coefficient of friction will be lowered and the wear rate will be decreased (potentially by up to an order of magnitude) relative to the untreated high-entropy alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy lacking Mo addition.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected to be maintained across the wide service temperature range typical of self-lubricating moving components, as long as the operating conditions promote the formation and stability of the MoO2 layer.
generation.uncertainty: The precise improvement magnitude and optimal Mo content require experimental calibration; effects may vary with processing details and specific service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy samples: one group with the targeted Mo addition and one control group without Mo. Subject both groups to identical ball-on-disk sliding tests across the stated temperature range under fixed load and sliding speed conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a tribometer
Wear rate assessed by measuring wear track volume or mass loss
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS, XPS) to verify the formation of a MoO2 lubricious layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped samples do not show a statistically significant and reproducible decrease in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control, or if no evidence of a lubricious MoO2 layer is observed on the wear surface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The results reveal that the Mo content significantly affects the microstructure, hardness, fracture toughness, and tribological behavior of the coatings. As the Mo content in the coatings increases gradually, the preferred orientation changes from (200) to (111). The coatings consistently exhibit a distinct columnar structure. Additionally, the hardness of the coatings increases from 24.39 to 30.24 GPa, along with an increase in fracture toughness. The friction coefficient is reduced from 0.72 to 0.26, and the wear rate is reduced by 10 times. During the friction process, the inter-column regions of the coatings are initially damaged, causing the wear track to exhibit a wavy pattern. Greater frictional heat is generated at the crest of the wave, resulting in the formation of a MoO2 lubricating layer. The friction reaction helps to reduce the shear force during friction, demonstrating the lower friction coefficient of the (AlCrTiZrMox)N coatings. In this study, we successfully synthesized a transition metal dichalcogenide high entropy alloy of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 with 2D structure and tested its tribological properties by performing ball‐on‐disk friction experiments using steel against steel tribopair in an ambient environment. The lubricant was coated onto the steel substrate by the conventional air spray coating process. The lubricant displayed excellent tribological properties with low average coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates of ≈0.076 and 2.6 × 10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1, respectively, at the high load of 9 N (contact pressure: 0.936 GPa). The analyses performed on the wear track and wear debris indicate stress‐induced tribocatalytic activity that facilitates the self‐lubricating behavior of HEA nanoflakes during friction tests performed in ambient conditions.
